Ignorant
ĭg´no-rant
adj. (destitute of knowledge; rendering Hebrew ba'ar, Greek agnoeo, idiotes)
From Latin ignorans, not knowing, from in-, not, and gnarus, knowing. Scripture distinguishes sharply between innocent lack of learning and culpable refusal to know.

Biblical Definition

Ignorant carries two very different weights in Scripture. There is ignorance that is no sin at all: Peter and John were reckoned “unlearned and ignorant men” by the council, and the text turns the insult into a commendation — “they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13). Formal learning is not godliness, and its absence is not disqualification. But there is also a culpable ignorance which Scripture treats as guilt: Israel, “being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness” (Rom 10:3) — ignorance that is a form of self-assertion, not of innocence. Isaiah's watchmen are the worst case: blind, ignorant, “dumb dogs, they cannot bark” (Isa 56:10), shepherds ignorant of the very danger they were posted to announce. Asaph, meanwhile, models the honest confession of it — “So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee” (Psa 73:22) — said not of his schooling but of his envy of the wicked.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ignorant as destitute of knowledge, uninstructed or uninformed, and notes the sense of being unacquainted with a particular thing — distinguishing want of instruction from want of understanding.

expand to see more

IG´NORANT, a. Destitute of knowledge; uninstructed or uninformed; untaught; unenlightened.

2. Unacquainted with; unknowing; as ignorant of the passage.

3. Unknown; undiscovered; a sense not now in use.

4. Done through ignorance; as an ignorant error.

Key Scripture

Act 4:13 — "Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus."

Rom 10:3 — "For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God."

Isa 56:10 — "His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber."

Psa 73:22 — "So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee."

Modern Corruption

Credentials mistaken for competence in the things of God, so that the unlearned believer is silenced — while the culpable ignorance Scripture actually condemns, ignorance of God's righteousness, goes unnoticed in the learned.

expand to see more

Acts 4:13 is a permanent rebuke to intellectual gatekeeping in the church. The council's assessment was accurate — these men were unlearned — and entirely beside the point, because they had been with Jesus. Wherever the ordinary believer is taught that Scripture is too difficult for him without a scholar's mediation, the Reformation's recovery of the open Bible is being quietly reversed, and the priesthood of all believers with it.

The opposite abuse is to make ignorance a virtue and study a suspicion, which Scripture never does. The ignorance it condemns is not unlettered but willful: Romans 10:3 describes men with every advantage of Scripture who did not know God's righteousness because they were busy constructing their own. That ignorance is compatible with immense learning. Isaiah's watchmen were the qualified men, and their qualification is precisely what makes their silence damnable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ba'ar (H1198), brutish, like a beast — Asaph's self-description; Greek agnoeo (G50), not to know; idiotes (G2399), a private unskilled man — the council's word for the apostles.

expand to see more

Hebrew ba'ar (H1198) — brutish, stupid as cattle; Asaph's confession that envy had reduced him to a beast before God (Psa 73:22).

Greek agnoeo (G50) — to be ignorant, not to understand; Paul's repeated I would not have you ignorant makes doctrine a pastoral duty (Rom 11:25; 1Co 10:1).

Greek idiotes (G2399) — a private person, unskilled, a layman; applied to Peter and John by the Sanhedrin (Act 4:13).

Usage

"“Unlearned and ignorant men… they had been with Jesus” — the insult becomes the commendation."

"“Being ignorant of God's righteousness” — the ignorance that is self-assertion."

"“They are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs” — watchmen who cannot bark."
